food.text: In the 1880s, famines pushed rural people into Moroccan cities in search of opportunities. Tea spread through wider segments of the population at that time, because it worked as an emergency calorie substitute and an appetite suppressant.

Couscous was integrated into French and European cuisine at the beginning of the twentieth century. It travelled through the French colonial empire and the Pieds-Noirs of Algeria. A staple of Algeria, Tunisia, Mauritania, Morocco and Libya, it reached European tables in this way.

After the French invasion of Algiers in 1830, Algerian migrants moved to Tétouan. According to the historian Idriss Bouhlila, they brought the dish pastilla and the werqa dough used to make it. From Tétouan it spread to the rest of Morocco sometime after 1830.

In the twenty years after the Anglo-Moroccan Treaty of 1856, tea imports to Morocco quadrupled. The British East India Company had also diverted tea meant for the Baltic states to Morocco during the Crimean War. Even so, tea consumption remained an urban practice.
Sugar and tea arrived from Europe at the port of Essaouira. Jewish merchants, who had started migrating to coastal cities in the 19th century, managed their passage through the interior of Morocco.

Among urban Moroccans, taking part in the tea ceremony became a symbol of status and savoir faire. Rural farmers, who both envied and resented the urban class, used tea drinking as a way to emulate it.

Historians believe pastilla entered northern Morocco through Ottoman Algeria, thanks to relations between the two regions in the 18th and 19th century. Bouhlila says the dish's name is of Turkish origin. This may explain why many inhabitants of northern Morocco called the dish Turkish.
The English traveller James Richardson recorded a description of a Moroccan tea ceremony in the 1840s. He said that during his travels tea was drunk widely and all day long.

art.text: After France invaded Tunisia in 1881, it built a new planned city outside the walls of Tunis instead of rebuilding the old one. The old city became known as the medina and the new one as the Ville Nouvelle. This contrasted with Algiers, where the French demolished much of the old city after 1830.

Berber women in the Maghreb wore silver jewellery that was cast in a mould and finished by hand. It included elaborate triangular plates and pins, originally used as clasps for garments, as well as necklaces, bracelets and earrings. Handed down from generation to generation, it was a visual element of Berber ethnic identity.

European architects in Tunisia often designed buildings in what they considered the "Arab" style. This ranged from extravagant pastiches of Moorish architecture to more academic designs based on study of the country's indigenous architecture. Called arabisant, it appeared in railway stations, post offices, law courts and some private villas.

The Carthage National Museum was founded in 1875 by the White Fathers of Cardinal Charles Martial Lavigerie as the "Musée Saint-Louis". It sits in the Chapelle Saint-Louis de Carthage and was created to house the finds of Alfred Louis Delattre's excavations. From 1899 to 1956 it was called the Museum Lavigerie.

The French collector and art critic Paul Eudel was one of the first to write art historical descriptions of Maghreb jewellery. His first account, L'orfévrerie algérienne et tunisienne, appeared in 1902. In 1906 he published a dictionary covering Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Tripolitaine, based on his travels and illustrated with graphics.
tags: Dictionnaire des bijoux de l'Afrique du Nord

art.text: Enamelled Berber jewellery was produced in Algeria (Great Kabylia), Morocco (Tiznit and the Anti-Atlas) and Tunisia (Moknine and the island of Djerba). Art historians say the cloisonné enamelling technique was introduced by Sephardi Jewish goldsmiths, who inherited the skill from their forefathers in Moorish Al-Andalus.

The Mosque of Yusuf Sahib al-Taba' in Tunis, built between 1808 and 1814, was one of the last and most impressive Husaynid-era mosques. It was built for one of Hamuda's ministers, and its decoration mixed local and European influences.

Father Delattre was sent to Carthage from 1875 by Cardinal Lavigerie with an apostolic and an archaeological purpose. He was particularly interested in Punic necropolises and Christian basilicas. Under the early French protectorate, the Bey of Tunis also signed a decree creating the National Museum of Bardo.

The Acropolium, a massive structure on Byrsa hill in Carthage, was built at the end of the 19th century. It stands on the presumed site of the tomb of King Louis IX (Saint Louis), who died there during the Eighth Crusade. His remains were repatriated to France, so the tomb is empty.

The Dar Batha palace in Fes, built in the late 19th century and now a museum, is a large and clear example of a classic riad. A riad is a rectangular garden divided into four quadrants by two paths, usually with a fountain at the centre. Riads became common in Fes only in recent centuries.

war.text: The Barbary Wars were a series of two wars fought by the United States, Sweden and the Kingdom of Sicily against the Barbary states, including Tunis, Algiers and Tripoli, and Morocco. The First Barbary War ran from 10 May 1801 to 10 June 1805. The Second lasted only three days, ending on 19 June 1815.

The Barbary Wars were the first major American wars fought entirely outside the New World, and in the Arab world. Since the 16th century, North African pirates had captured ships and raided European coastal areas, first to capture non-Muslim slaves for the North African slave trade, later to kidnap people for ransom. By the 19th century pirate activity had declined, but Barbary pirates still demanded tribute from American merchant vessels in the Mediterranean. Refusal to pay meant the capture of American ships and goods, and often the enslavement or ransoming of crew members.

The Battle of Isly was fought on August 14, 1844, between France and Morocco near the Isly River. French forces under Marshal Thomas Robert Bugeaud routed a much larger but poorly organized Moroccan force, mainly fighters from the tribes of Beni Snassen, but also from the Beni Angad and Beni Oukil, under Muhammad, son of the Sultan of Morocco, Abd al-Rahman. The Moroccans had 800 of their men killed, while the French had 27 killed and 99 wounded.

After Thomas Jefferson became president in March 1801, he sent a U.S. Navy fleet to the Mediterranean to combat the Barbary pirates. The fleet bombarded numerous fortified cities in present-day Libya, Tunisia and Algeria. Among the fleet's ships, the Philadelphia ran aground on an uncharted reef off Tripoli while under fire from shore batteries and Tripolitan gunboats. Its crew was taken prisoner and enslaved, and the ship was later destroyed by a raiding party led by Stephen Decatur. The fleet ultimately extracted concessions of safe conduct from the Barbary states, which ended the first war.

Bugeaud was trying to complete the French conquest of Algeria when he instigated the Battle of Isly without a declaration of war. He wanted to force negotiations over Moroccan support for the Algerian resistance leader Abd el-Kader to end on terms favorable to France. The French demanded that the Sultan of Morocco withdraw that support.

Since the Invasion of Algiers in 1830, Emir Abd el-Kader led the tribes of the Mascara region against the French, from 1832. In 1837 Marshal Bugeaud signed the Treaty of Tafna with him. Abd el-Kader had to recognize French sovereignty in North Africa, while France recognized his authority over a large part of Algeria.

When war broke out between America and Britain in 1812, the British regent, George IV, wrote to Dey Haji Ali Pasha of Algiers. He confirmed the bonds of friendship between the two countries and declared Britain ready to defend Algiers against every aggressor. His aim was to win Algiers over against America, or at least keep it neutral.

Under Dey Omar Pasha, American-Algerian relations worsened when he demanded an increase in the annual tribute. The Americans went to Algiers to fight under Commodore Stephen Decatur, which culminated in the Battle off Cape Gata and the death of the famous corsair captain Raïs Hamidou. A letter to the dey on April 12, 1815 told him America had decided to go to war against him, after reminding him of the horrors of war. In the end the dey was forced to pay $10,000 in compensation and to renounce all that America had been paid.

At Isly, Bugeaud recovered the Moroccan commander's tent and umbrella, equivalent to capturing a military standard in European warfare. The French also captured eleven pieces of artillery, eighteen flags and all the Moroccan tents, while 800 Moroccans were killed against 27 French killed and 99 wounded. For his victory Bugeaud was made Duke of Isly.

In 1843, following the Battle of the Smala, Abd el-Kader saw his mobile encampment at Taguin destroyed. He was driven back into the desert and took refuge in Morocco. That brought Sultan Abd al-Rahman's army into conflict with France at Isly.
The day after the Battle of Isly, the Bombardment of Mogador started. The French fleet bombarded the ports of Tangier and Mogador while Sultan Abd al-Rahman's army was being defeated at Isly.

The Sultan of Morocco, Abd al-Rahman, tried to seize Tlemcen from the French in October 1830. He sent 5,000 cavalry and infantry, who rampaged through the streets, looting and fighting. Facing French diplomatic and naval pressure, the Sultan eventually had to withdraw them.

literature.text: The Nahda, a literary and cultural revival, spread through Arab-populated regions including Tunisia during the second half of the 19th century and into the early 20th century. Its writers largely kept to classical Arabic literary forms while addressing modern themes and the challenges facing Arab societies of the era.

Algerian religious and military leader Emir Abdelkader led resistance against France from 1831 to 1847, then settled in Damascus in 1855 after his release. It was there that he wrote his major literary work, the Kitab al-Mawaqif, or 'Book of Halts'.

Since the beginning of the 19th century, Kabyle intellectuals in Algeria began writing their Berber language using the Latin script under French influence. This became the basis for the modern Berber Latin alphabet still used today.

Gustave Flaubert published his novel Salammbô in 1858, which helped fuel a "fashion of irresistible attraction" for Carthage. Earlier, in 1833, the Danish consul Christian Tuxen Falbe had drawn the first topography of the remains in his Recherches sur l'emplacement de Carthage.

Emir Abdelkader issued strict orders to his soldiers not to mishandle or disrespect books and manuscripts. Breaking this rule was severely punished, showing how highly he valued written works even during his war against the French colonizers.

Beyond protecting books, Emir Abdelkader built schools across the villages, towns and cities of his emirate. He chose qualified teachers and supported them both financially and morally, paying wages based on their qualifications.

Emir Abdelkader rewarded his soldiers whenever they brought him a book or its author, rather than merely tolerating such finds. This turned his protection of manuscripts into an active incentive within his own army.
Copying a single manuscript could take several months in Emir Abdelkader's Algeria. This was a long delay for the Emir, given his ongoing war against the French colonizers.

When the fortress of Tagdemt fell to French invaders, Emir Abdelkader moved his stored books and manuscripts to his own encampment, known as the Smala, for safekeeping. French soldiers seized them anyway after the Battle of the Smala in 1843.

science.text: At the time of the French conquest of Algeria in 1830, literacy rates there were higher than those of European France. Zawiyas, institutions tied to Sufi orders, were the primary sources of education. They taught basic literacy to a large proportion of children, even in remote mountainous areas.

The recording industry emerged in the Maghreb in the late 19th century. According to historian Christopher Silver, the limited playing time of 78 rpm records forced traditional Arabic compositions to be condensed. In this way the technology itself reshaped musical practice.

Christian Tuxen Falbe, the consul of Denmark, drew the first topography of the remains of Carthage. It appeared in his Recherches sur l'emplacement de Carthage, published in 1833, and belonged to an early 19th-century era of pioneering travelers and visionaries.

A student at a zawiya who was apt enough could move beyond the Qur'an to law, theology and Arabic grammar. The curriculum also included mathematics, mainly as it applied to the complex legal system of inheritance distribution, and sometimes astronomy.

Charles Ernest Beulé highlighted the Roman apses on the hill of Byrsa at Carthage, but quickly met the difficulties of excavating a space that had been reworked many times. He predicted that "Carthage will have its turn, like Egypt, like Nineveh, and like Babylon."

Silver argued that the recording industry also contributed to stylistic changes in Maghrebi music, including faster performances. It also encouraged the adoption of Western instruments such as the piano and harmonium.

During the first years of the French protectorate, the Bey of Tunis signed several decrees. One created the National Museum of Bardo, and another regulated excavations and protected the heritage of Tunisia.

In an October 1858 letter to Ernest Feydeau, Gustave Flaubert wrote that "we know nothing about Carthage." The city had been pillaged, then forgotten, and only later did archaeologists begin to recover its story.

politics.text: Morocco stayed independent under Alawi rule until 1912. That year the Treaty of Fes started a French protectorate in central Morocco and a Spanish protectorate in the north and south. The Alawi sultans continued as nominal monarchs under French colonial rule.
The French conquest of Algeria in 1830 disrupted regional stability. After it, Morocco faced serious challenges from European encroachment in the region.
Between 1848 and 1865, Britain, France and Spain competed for influence in Morocco. Britain wanted to keep France at bay, especially since Morocco was next to Gibraltar.

British consul John Hay Drummond Hay pressured Abd ar-Rahman into signing the Anglo-Moroccan Treaty of 1856. It removed government restrictions on trade and gave Britain special privileges, including a protégé system that let Britain extend legal protection to individuals within Morocco.
Sultan Abdelaziz appointed his brother Abdelhafid as viceroy of Marrakesh. Abdelhafid then sought to overthrow him by stirring distrust over Abdelaziz's European ties.
In the Italo-Turkish War of 1911, the Ottoman Empire lost its North African territories. It also lost the Dodecanese in that conflict.
Spain's government was eager to expand its presence in Africa to distract from its own domestic difficulties. The Hispano-Moroccan War followed, lasting from 1859 to 1860.

After the Hispano-Moroccan War, the Treaty of Wad Ras obliged Morocco to pay off its war debt to Spain. To do so, the Moroccan government took a massive British loan that was larger than its national reserves.

During the Hafidiya of 1907 to 1908, Abdelaziz reigned from Rabat while Abdelhafid reigned in Marrakesh and Fez. Abdelaziz was defeated in battle in 1908, and in 1909 Abdelhafid became the recognized leader of Morocco.

A late 19th-century French source estimated that in 1880 Algeria had 355 zawiyas, Sufi institutions, with 167,019 members. That was out of a population of slightly less than three million Muslims. During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, colonial governments confiscated waqf properties or marginalized the waqf system, to diminish the zawiyas' power.

In his bid for the throne, Abdelhafid was aided by Madani el-Glaoui, older brother of T'hami, one of the Caids of the Atlas. A British officer named Andrew Belton, a veteran of the Second Boer War, helped train his troops.

philosophy.text: French colonialism in Algeria gave rise to the Kabyle myth in the early to mid 19th century. It was a set of beliefs about a fundamental distinction between Arabs and Kabyles. French writers claimed the Kabyle people were more predisposed than Arabs to assimilate into "French civilization".

By the 19th century, zawiyas, the Sufi institutions serving as places of worship and religious instruction, had large and widespread memberships across the Maghreb. The Sanusiyya tariqa, for example, was widespread and influential in Libya and the eastern Sahara regions.

In 1847 Eugène Daumas and Paul-Dieudonné Fabar wrote that "Beneath the Muslim peel, one finds a Christian seed." They claimed the Kabyles, once entirely Christian, still displayed the symbol of the Cross, unbeknownst to them, in their facial tattoos.

Early European writings often portrayed Kabyles as closer to Mediterranean or European societies. After the Mokrani Revolt in 1871, the discourse shifted to depict them as violent and inferior. This shift accompanied a colonial justification for the repression and atrocities carried out by French colonial forces.

A late 19th-century French source estimated that in 1880 there were 355 zawiyas in Algeria. Their membership was 167,019, out of a population of slightly less than three million Muslims in the country.

The Kabyle myth was seriously elaborated by French colonists between 1840 and 1857, largely in the writings of military men such as Baron Aucapitaine and Adolphe Hanoteau. It was diffused between 1860 and 1871, then reached its climax between 1871 and 1892.

The French colony judged the Kabyles more ready to assimilate because of the supposed democratic nature of their society, their superficial Islamicization, and the higher status of Kabyle women. It also believed they were ancient Christians of Celtic origin who could easily be re-Christianized.

In Tunisia, many zawiyas were patronized and supported by the government of the Husaynid beys. Elsewhere, colonial occupations split the Sufi orders: some zawiyas collaborated with the authorities while others resisted.

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, colonial governments in North Africa confiscated waqf properties or marginalized the waqf system. These charitable endowments financed the zawiyas, so the move was a way of diminishing their power and influence.
In Tunisia, the government of the Husaynid beys patronized and supported many zawiyas. Elsewhere, the Sanusiyya tariqa was widespread and influential in Libya and the eastern Sahara regions.

culture.text: For centuries the Jews of Tunisia were forced to wear a garment called the shikla, whose main goal was to distinguish and humiliate them in public spaces. In 888 Ibrahim ibn Ahmad reportedly ordered Jews to wear a patch showing a monkey and Christians one showing a pig. Later, Muhammad al-Uqbani reported that those who disobeyed were given twenty lashes and thrown into prison, and a second offence meant brutal beatings and indefinite imprisonment. The shikla ended with the Pacte fondamental, following a decree of Mohammed Bey on 14 September 1858, which also let Jews wear the Red Chéchia headpiece like other Tunisians.

In the early 19th century, interest in Carthage grew into what the article calls a "fashion of irresistible attraction". A historical and archaeological society was born in Paris and aroused interest. The fashion reached a certain culmination with Gustave Flaubert's publication of Salammbô in 1858.

Spanish and French colonization beginning in the 19th century made Roman Catholicism grow in Morocco. The growth was mainly among the European colonists themselves. A small number of Moroccans with origins in these two countries remain in Morocco.

For centuries the Jews of Tunisia were forced to wear a distinguishing garment called the shikla, meant to distinguish and humiliate them in public. Under the Almohad ruler Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur in 1198 even Jews who had converted to Islam had to wear it, because he doubted their conversion was sincere. The Flemish traveller Anselm Adornes reported that the Jews of Tunis wore a piece of yellow cloth on head and neck, without which they would be stoned. The Pacte fondamental, which followed the decree of Mohammed Bey on 14 September 1858, removed dhimmi status, and Jews could then wear the Red Chéchia headpiece like other Tunisians.

The Danish consul Christian Tuxen Falbe drew the first topography of the remains of Carthage. He published it in 1833 in his Recherches sur l'emplacement de Carthage. The article calls the early 19th century the age of pioneers, both travelers and visionaries.
Under French colonial rule, Algeria was home to 1.4 million pieds-noirs, mostly Catholic ethnic French settlers, while Morocco and Tunisia also had sizeable European populations.

Gustave Flaubert wrote to Ernest Feydeau in October 1858 that "we know nothing about Carthage." The city had been pillaged and then forgotten after the turmoil of the Mediterranean world. That same year, Flaubert published his novel Salammbô.

When the shikla was abolished in Tunisia, Ibn Abi Dhiaf wrote about the decision. He argued that prescribing specific attire for the people of the "dhimma" has nothing to do with the foundations of religion. He noted that the Prophet never changed the dress of the Jews of Medina.

Cardinal Charles Lavigerie established the Carthage National Museum in 1875. Charles Ernest Beulé and Alfred Louis Delattre carried out excavations at Carthage in the second half of the 19th century, and the Danish consul Christian Tuxen Falbe had conducted the first examination of the site in 1830. French archaeologists' excavations in the 1920s drew great attention because of the proof they seemed to give of child sacrifice at Carthage, though whether children were sacrificed in ancient Carthage has been intensely debated among researchers.

The sign of Tanit, a symbol of the Punic goddess Tanit, was first reported in the beginning of the 19th century. It appeared on stele unearthed at the site of Carthage. Modern scholars associate it with Tanit, partner of Ba'al Hammon.
